DraftKings NFL DFS Cheat Sheet: Week 1 Picks And Stacks

By Sam Smith

September 7, 2026 · Updated September 11, 2026

The free DraftKings NFL DFS cheat sheet from Stokastic covers the 12-game Week 1 main slate Sunday, Sept. 13, and Friday's pull moved the board in one direction: the Sims are backing away from the slate's top projection and putting the leverage into running backs the field has written off. Jahmyr Gibbs lost 10 points of exposure overnight, Chuba Hubbard took over the leverage panel from 1.6% ownership, and Michael Mayer turned into the second-most-owned player on the slate. I swap two seats and re-price the whole build under the $50,000 cap below.

Refreshed Sept. 11: every panel re-pulled from the Stokastic Sims for the DraftKings main slate, with projections stamped 2:04 p.m. ET and ownership 2:07 p.m. ET. Carolina's Friday injury report is in, Zay Flowers was reported upgraded to full participation on the Ravens' second report of the week, and the worked build swaps two seats.

The Quick Answer

Gibbs is still first in projection at 24.8 and still the play at $8,000, but own him knowing the Sims cut him: 41.0% exposure against 53.0% projected ownership. The new leverage lead is Chuba Hubbard at $5,500, 1.6% owned with 7.0% exposure, after Carolina's Friday report came back without his name on it. Michael Mayer ($2,900) is still the slate's top value at 4.06 but he is chalk now at 29.0% owned. Stack the Bengals, in 7.6% of top lineups. The full board, the Friday news behind it, and the build that fits Gibbs and Hubbard in the same lineup are below.

Panels as of Sept. 11; re-check before lock. The row that rewrote this edition is the leverage panel, and Hubbard's line is the reason. He is projected for 14.1 points at $5,500 with 1.6% of the field on him, and the Stokastic Sims, which play the slate tens of thousands of times with ownership modeled as a distribution, put him in 7.0% of their top lineups. Leverage is exposure minus projected ownership, so that gap is plus 5.4%, the widest on the board and more than two full points clear of the next name. Sept. 10's panel was led by a bigger number, Swift's 6.3%, but Swift is a 7.0%-owned back today; this edge belongs to a player almost nobody has rostered. I come back to exactly how many of my 20 lineups carry him at the end.

What Moved Since Sept. 10

Hubbard's number is a Friday-news number. He hurt a hamstring in training camp and was called week-to-week, so Carolina spent August talking about a committee with Jonathon Brooks. Then the Panthers' Friday injury report landed: Brooks was a full participant with no game designation, and Hubbard was not on the report at all. The ownership model has not repriced it: 1.6% is where a back sits when the market still remembers the hamstring, and nothing I have seen built since Friday morning says otherwise.

Hubbard's clearance is why the top of that panel changed hands, and the shape underneath it says more than his line does: four of the five leverage names are running backs, and the new one, the Saints' Travis Etienne Jr. at plus 2.9%, is a co-starter with Alvin Kamara. That is the same structure as Carolina's. In four different games, the model is paying for Week 1 backfields the field refuses to price because nobody will promise them a workload. The movers: Swift led the panel at 6.3% on Sept. 10 and now sits fourth at plus 2.6%, Marvin Harrison Jr. was second at 3.5% and has dropped out of the top five at plus 0.9%, and two names survived both pulls — Swift, and Chase Brown, who was third at 3.0% on Sept. 10 and is second at plus 3.2% today.

The top of the board moved the other way. Gibbs' projection came down from 26.3 to 24.8 and his exposure fell from 51.1% to 41.0% while the field only trimmed him from 57.5% to 53.0%, so his leverage went from minus 6.4% to minus 12.0% — the most negative number on the slate by a distance. Nothing is wrong with him: Detroit is essentially healthy into the opener and Gibbs is the clear lead back with David Montgomery now in Houston. They simply stopped paying his price as often. Michael Mayer went the same direction from the opposite end, climbing from 23.2% to 29.0% owned, which makes a $2,900 tight end the second-most-owned player on the slate.

The stack panel compressed with them. Cincinnati still leads but at 7.6% rather than 11.4%, and Detroit, second at 9.9% on Sept. 10, is fourth at 4.3% — the Sims are building Gibbs by himself now, not the Lions' passing game around him. Baltimore moved up to second at 5.2%, and Zay Flowers was reported upgraded from limited Wednesday to a full participant on the Ravens' next report; he carries plus 2.0% leverage at $6,400.

Running Back: The Leverage Left Chicago For Carolina

DraftKings is full PPR with 3-point bonuses at 100 rushing, 100 receiving and 300 passing yards, and in a full-PPR scoring system a cleared committee back at $5,500 is a genuinely different asset than the field is treating him as. Hubbard projects 14.1; Brooks, playing the same backfield, projects 8.9 at $5,000 and 0.4% ownership. The Sims are not splitting Carolina down the middle — they are picking a side, and it is the side that did not need a Friday designation.

Swift is the version of this bet the field already found, at 7.0% ownership with 9.6% exposure. The cramp that pulled him out of a Sept. 3 practice was reported as nothing and he practiced after, so he remains a positive-leverage back at 15.4 projected. The difference is price and crowd: Swift costs $600 more than Hubbard for 1.3 more projected points at more than four times the ownership. I want the cheaper one, and the gap between what the field pays for each of them is the leverage you get paid for.

Tight End: Mayer Is Still Right, And Now Everyone Knows

With Brock Bowers out after a Sept. 9 meniscus trim, Mayer is the Raiders' starting tight end at $2,900, and at 4.06 he is the best value on the board by half a point. Read his row honestly, though: 29.0% owned against 22.6% exposure is minus 6.4% leverage, the second-worst on the slate behind Gibbs. You play Mayer because the $2,400 you save against Colston Loveland ($5,300) is what pays for a Bengals stack and two backs, not because the field is missing him.

Trey McBride is the opposite profile at $6,800: the only tight end on the slate projected above 14, at 5.9% ownership with plus 1.0% leverage. He is a perfectly good contrarian tight end and I have him in zero of my 20, which is the honest version of this. The $3,900 gap up to him has to come out of a starting back, and the backs are where the Sims put their whole edge this week — four of the top five leverage names. The Mayer discount is what lets Hubbard and Chase Brown sit in the same lineup, and I am not trading one of them for a tight end.

Worked Example: The Bengals Stack Under The Cap

The Bengals stack shows up in 7.6% of top lineups, more than any other team; that is Cincinnati's stack rate, not a vote for this exact trio. This build lands on $49,800 with a 138.5 projection:

  1. Stack: Burrow ($6,900), Ja'Marr Chase ($7,800) and Chase Brown ($7,100). Chase is 28.3% owned, third on the slate at minus 5.2% leverage; Brown is 7.2% owned with 10.4% exposure, the second-best leverage on the board, so the stack runs a receiver the field loves through a back it is skipping. Tee Higgins ($6,300) is the conventional second piece, and the reason he is out is price, not his minus 0.6% leverage: his salary is the money that buys Hubbard.
  2. Chalk: Gibbs ($8,000). His leverage is minus 12.0%, but 24.8 is 2.9 points clear of Bijan Robinson's 21.9, and in one lineup the top projection stays in.
  3. FLEX: Hubbard ($5,500), the top leverage play at plus 5.4%, off Friday's injury report entirely and still 1.6% owned.
  4. The rest: Luther Burden III ($5,500, plus 2.1% leverage, the Bears side of Hubbard's game), Devaughn Vele ($3,500, the Saints bring-back against Gibbs that frees the salary), Mayer ($2,900) and the Falcons ($2,600, plus 0.8% leverage). The Dolphins are the higher-leverage defense at plus 1.2%, but they play the Raiders, and I will not roster a defense against my own tight end.

Two spots changed from the Sept. 10 build: Swift out for Hubbard, Harrison Jr. out for Burden. The Falcons-over-Dolphins call is the same one for the same reason, and the other seven seats carried over, which is what a two-swap week looks like when the board moves everywhere but only the leverage panel changes a seat. Price the rest of it from the Week 1 pricing breakdown. Confirm Hubbard's game-day status before lock: a back with no Friday designation is usually a back who plays, but Carolina has described the backfield as a committee to start the year, and the NFL DFS projections, ownership and stacks in the DataHub update through Sunday morning. Where My Entries Land

The Sept. 10 read was a chalk-heavy week with the leverage at running back. Friday's board says the same thing louder, and it moved the running back. Gibbs lands in 8 of my 20 entries, down from 10, right on the Sims' 41.0% and well under the field's 53.0%; the 12 without him start from Bijan Robinson at $7,700, the only other back inside the top five projections the Sims hold above the field at plus 1.6%. Hubbard is in 5 of the 20 — more than three times the Sims' 7.0% and about 16 times the field's 1.6% — because a cleared back nobody has re-read the injury report on is the rarest thing a Week 1 board can hand you, and Chase Brown, one of the two names that survived both pulls, gets 4. Swift, the other, gets 3 at his higher price and higher ownership. The Bengals pairing of Burrow and Chase is my single entry and 5 of the 20, with Brown riding in four of those five and Baltimore behind it at 3.
